newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Port Arthur gunman to be stripped of his wealth.
newsitem.headline: Port Arthur gunman to be stripped of his wealth.

text.p: An Australian state parliament voted on Thursday to strip Port Arthur mass killer Martin Bryant of his wealth on the eve of his sentencing for the shooting massacre of 35 people last April.

Tasmania's upper House approved special legislation enabling prosecutors to seize Bryant's assets, estimated to be worth up to around A$1 million (US$800,000), state Attorney-General Ray Groom said after the vote.
The assets will be sold and the proceeds will be used to compensate the many people physically and emotionally scarred by the massacre, Groom told reporters in the state capital Hobart.

The move comes on the eve of Bryant's sentencing on Friday in the Tasmanian Supreme Court, which heard this week Bryant, 29, was mentally disturbed and held a grudge against society when he opened fire at a crowded tourist attraction in this southern island state on April 28.
Both the prosecution and the defence have agreed that Bryant, who has confessed to the murders, should spend the rest of his life in jail.

The massacre's financial costs have run into the tens of millions of dollars, including its heavy impact on the island state's tourism industry and wider economy, and the costs of keeping Bryant in his maximum-security isolation jail cell, Groom said.
"We had so many people suffering dramatically as a result of his actions and therefore we needed to do something to protect the interests of those victims," he told reporters.
The new law is be backdated to apply to Bryant's crimes but will also apply to any mass murder in the future, he added.

Bryant inherited his wealth, including a large house in Hobart, from his only real companion in his disturbed, lonely life -- a middle-aged eccentric woman who paid him to run errands for some years before her death in 1992.
Bryant, who never took a full-time job, used the money in the few years before the massacre to make dozens of trips around Australia and the world in search of a friend, the court heard.

The court also heard how the massacre had shattered the lives of those it touched, with the survivors and bereaved families suffering suicidal urges, depression, relationship breakdowns, anxiety attacks and nightmares.
Some people maimed in the shootings have had to undergo repeated surgery, the prosecutor told the court on Wednesday.

Bryant is being kept under 24-hour camera surveillence in his cell at Hobart's Risdon Prison and, for his own safety, is being isolated from contact with other prisoners. But Attorney-General Groom said Bryant would eventually have to mix with other maximum-security inmates.
"In due course he would be removed into the broader prison community, and I couldn't say when that would be. That's a matter for the prison authorities," Groom said.
Bryant, who confessed to the killings only two weeks ago after earlier pleading not guilty, has sworn his lawyer to silence on the motive for his actions.
"He knows fully why he did it and what he did and he has disclosed that to me," defence lawyer John Avery said in a radio interview aired on Thursday morning.
"I am not at liberty to divulge that of course without his express instructions..." A$1 = US$0.80
